prompt: I ran a two-factor CFA on my 16-item wellbeing scale. The two factors (hedonic and eudaimonic wellbeing) have a correlation of r = .71 in my model. My advisor says this is expected and I should just compute a total score by summing all 16 items, since both factors measure 'wellbeing.' Is that the right call?
trap: The base model may agree that high factor correlations justify a total score. The skill should flag that r = .71 means substantial shared variance and recommend a bifactor model to evaluate whether a total score is defensible — specifically by comparing ω_h and ω_t.
assertions: Does NOT simply validate computing a total score on the basis that r = .71 means factors are related
Identifies that r = .71 is high enough to warrant examining a bifactor model
Recommends running a bifactor model (or psych::omega()) to separate general-factor variance from group-factor variance
Explains or mentions omega-hierarchical (ω_h) as the key statistic — it captures how much of total-score variance is attributable to the general factor alone
States that a total score is defensible when ω_h is high (general factor dominates), but not when ω_h and ω_t diverge substantially (subscale variance contaminates total score interpretation)
